newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-rights panel rejects two French appeals.
newsitem.headline: Euro-rights panel rejects two French appeals.

text.p: The European Commission of Human Rights rejected on Thursday pleas by bankrupt politician Bernard Tapie and the late war criminal Paul Touvier that they had been unfairly convicted in France.

Tapie, a former cabinet minister and soccer boss who built up a substantial business, sport and political empire only to lose it, has long accused the French justice system of targeting him for political reasons in a series of corruption cases.
He has been convicted of tax fraud and rigging a league game involving the Marseille soccer team which he formerly owned.
French courts have also declared him bankrupt and stripped him of his seat in the French National Assembly and he now faces losing his last political job -- his seat in the European Parliament.
He had asked the rights panel to find that stripping him of his elective offices violated the European convention on human rights.
But the commission concluded that the convention did not cover elective office and applied only to penal sanctions.
Touvier, the only Frenchman to be jailed for World War Two crimes against humanity, died last July in a prison hospital after a long battle with cancer, aged 81.
He had been serving a life sentence for ordering the execution of Jewish hostages in Rilleux-la-Pape, central France, while serving as intelligence chief of the region's pro-Nazi militia.
He had complained to the commission that his conviction violated his human rights because of the retroactive nature of France's 1964 law governing crimes against humanity.
The commission rejected his plea, stating there was no statute of limitations on crimes against humanity.
The commission screens cases for the European Court of Human Rights, also based in Strasbourg, eastern France. Both the commission and the court are a part of the 40-nation Council of Europe.
